extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, and mathematicians interested in history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A university news/feature piece describing the history, significance, and mathematical impact of a major result (Andrew Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem). Intended to explain historical context and research consequences to a broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and correctness of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Details of the proof remained to be thoroughly checked’ and ultimately ‘the proof as it stood contained a hole, which it took Wiles, together with the mathematician Richard Taylor, nearly a year to fix.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical proofs must be scrutinised and checked in detail; initial announcements may contain gaps that require correction. Community scrutiny and subsequent collaboration are normal and necessary to establish correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of results (proving in settings that imply target cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles proved the modularity conjecture 'in a setting that was general enough to imply that Fermat's Last Theorem was also true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving a more general statement that implies important special cases is a powerful strategy: it can settle multiple problems at once and often yields broader mathematical tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative approaches that add substantial mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that Wiles' method was 'a completely new approach' and that 'whether it succeeded or not, it had added a substantial amount to mathematics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel methods that bring new ideas or techniques into play are valuable in themselves; even attempts that do not immediately resolve a problem can substantially advance the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term commitment and working practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles worked 'alone and in secret, for a period of seven years.' The piece remarks: 'Very few people want to work on a problem for that long. To really commit yourself to a problem takes a certain kind of personality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep problems may require sustained, focused effort over many years; working privately can reduce distractions and unwanted attention but may limit early feedback and increase the risk of undetected errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting disparate fields as a measure of impact (Langlands programme)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Langlands programme 'draws extremely surprising connections between different fields of mathematics' and is described as 'the future of mathematics' that 'provides new tools for attacking problems in number theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that reveals deep connections across areas of mathematics and supplies tools usable elsewhere is especially impactful and is valued as advancing the broader research programme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solved problems often generate new research directions
rubrics_metrics.description: The article observes that 'a solved problem usually opens up a range of unsolved ones' and that Wiles' proof 'opened another door' leading to further progress in modularity and the Langlands programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contributions not only by the problem they solve but also by the new avenues of research they create; the capacity to stimulate subsequent work is a key sign of significance.
